title: CycleClear
question: How does a bicycle work?
hook: Two triangles, a chain and a wheel of thin wires, and a machine that balances itself. Take a bicycle apart in 3D and ride its physics.

explainer.title: A frame of two triangles
explainer.text: Most bikes use a diamond frame: two triangles sharing the seat tube. A triangle can't change shape unless one side changes length, so thin, light tubes make a stiff frame.

explainer.title: A chain links pedals to wheel
explainer.text: Your feet turn the cranks and the front chainring. The chain carries every tooth's movement to a small cog on the back wheel, so the wheel turns with you.

explainer.title: Gears trade effort for speed
explainer.text: The gear ratio is front teeth divided by rear teeth. A small rear cog gives more distance per pedal stroke but needs more force; a big one makes hills easier but slower.

explainer.title: A moving bike balances itself
explainer.text: When a moving bike leans, its front wheel steers into the lean, bringing the wheels back under it. Above about 15 km/h, many bikes catch every wobble on their own. Lock the handlebars and it falls.

explainer.title: Wheels hang on tensioned spokes
explainer.text: Every spoke is pulled tight to about 1,000 newtons. When you sit on the bike, only the spokes at the bottom change: they lose some tension. The rest hold the rim round.

explainer.title: Brakes turn motion into heat
explainer.text: Stopping means getting rid of kinetic energy, which grows with the square of speed. Brake pads grip a disc or rim and friction turns that energy into heat.

concepts.def: Front teeth divided by rear teeth: how many times the wheel turns for each turn of the pedals.
How fast you pedal, in revolutions per minute.
How far behind the steering axis the front tyre touches the ground. It helps the front wheel steer into a lean.
A moving bicycle's ability to correct a lean without a rider.
The pull built into every spoke, which lets thin wires carry a rider's weight.
The energy of motion, equal to half the mass times the speed squared.
A turning force: force multiplied by the length of the lever it pushes on.
